input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-509: Seminar in Computer Science. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: This course examines current topics in Computer Science. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course topics, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to no cluster; hence, such courses will count only as general Computer Science electives. Contact Hours: Lecture/Lab 3

Source excerpts:

[acm-code-of-ethics]
The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.

[acm-research-practice]
Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.

[rit-csci-509]
This course examines current topics in Computer Science. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course topics, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to no cluster; hence, such courses will count only as general Computer Science electives. Contact Hours: Lecture/Lab 3

beats.claim: CSCI-509 is designed as a faculty-piloted general Computer Science elective that examines current topics in the field.
beats.example: A department might use this course to test a new AI ethics module before adding it to the standard curriculum.
beats.title: Course Scope and Flexibility
beats.visualDirection: Display a flexible course outline template with placeholders for topics, prerequisites, and assessment methods.

beats.claim: Specific course details, including format, learning outcomes, and resource needs, are determined by the faculty member proposing the seminar.
beats.example: An instructor could adapt the course to focus on cybersecurity, machine learning, or software engineering based on departmental needs.
beats.title: Faculty Role and Customization
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist of customizable course parameters with checkboxes for each element.

beats.claim: Courses in this category are identified as belonging to no cluster and count only as general Computer Science electives.
beats.example: Students can enroll in CSCI-509 to fulfill general elective requirements without meeting specific cluster prerequisites.
beats.title: Cluster Classification
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a course catalog map showing CSCI-509 as a standalone elective node rather than a cluster member.

beats.claim: The ACM Code of Ethics directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being.
beats.example: Developing accessible software tools that help people with disabilities aligns with this ethical directive.
beats.title: ACM Ethics Foundation
beats.visualDirection: Present a circular diagram linking 'society' and 'human well-being' to core computing practices.

beats.claim: Computing professionals should avoid harm, be honest and trustworthy, and take action not to discriminate.
beats.example: Auditing an algorithm for biased training data and correcting it prevents discriminatory outcomes in hiring tools.
beats.title: Avoiding Harm and Honesty
beats.visualDirection: Show a balance scale with 'fairness' on one side and 'bias' on the other, emphasizing corrective action.

beats.claim: Professionals should respect the work required to produce new ideas, respect privacy, and honor confidentiality.
beats.example: Citing open-source libraries properly and encrypting user data in a mobile application demonstrates these values.
beats.title: Respecting Work and Privacy
beats.visualDirection: Display icons representing citation practices and data encryption alongside a respect symbol.

beats.claim: Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products, and maintain high standards of professional competence.
beats.example: Implementing rigorous code reviews and automated testing ensures both reliable software and sustainable development workflows.
beats.title: Quality and Security Standards
beats.visualDirection: Create a flowchart showing 'process quality' leading to 'product quality' with a competence badge.

beats.claim: Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence, cites prior work, and identifies the contribution being reported.
beats.example: A research paper clearly separates its novel algorithm from existing methods and explicitly states the new findings.
beats.title: Responsible Technical Communication
beats.visualDirection: Show a two-column layout: left for 'claims/evidence', right for 'contributions/prior work' with arrows linking them.

beats.claim: Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work, and results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion.
beats.example: Publishing raw data alongside statistical analysis allows independent verification of experimental outcomes.
beats.title: Methods and Results Integrity
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a magnifying glass over a methodology section and a graph with clear, unaltered axes.

beats.claim: Authors should preserve research integrity, avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification, and disclose conflicts of interest.
beats.example: Using reference managers to track citations and disclosing funding sources maintains academic honesty in computer science research.
beats.title: Research Integrity and Practical Analysis
beats.visualDirection: Provide a practical analysis checklist with items: 'Citations verified', 'Conflicts disclosed', 'Methods reproducible', 'Results accurate'.

Explain the ACM Code of Ethics principles that guide responsible computing practice.
Describe the core components of responsible technical communication in computer science research.
